h: Joseph and Benjamin Unite in Holiness

p: וַיִּפֹּל עַל צַוְּארֵי בִנְיָמִין אָחִיו וַיֵּבְךְּ וּבִנְיָמִן בָּכָה עַל צַוָּארָיו.
— ‘He fell upon the neck of Benjamin his brother and wept, and Benjamin wept upon his neck.’

h: The Altar Refines the Desire for Food

p: הִנֵּה הַמִּזְבֵּחַ נִקְרָא זְאֵב הַטּוֹרֵף שֶׁכֵּן קְרָאַתּוּ לוּקוֹס (סוֹף סוּכָּה)
— The altar is called a ravening wolf, for it was called lykos, ‘wolf,’ at the end of Sukkah.
וְהוּא עַל שֵׁם אֲכִילַת הַקָּרְבָּנוֹת שֶׁל הַבְּהֵמוֹת כְּדֵי לְבָרֵר כָּל מִינֵי אֲכִילוֹת שֶׁל נֶפֶשׁ הַבַּהֲמִית
— This refers to its consumption of animal offerings, which refines all forms of eating associated with the animal soul.
וְעֲבוּר זֶה נִקְרָא בִּנְיָמִין זְאֵב יִטְרָף שֶׁעַל כֵּן בָּנוּי בְּחֶלְקוֹ הַמִּזְבֵּחַ בְּבֵית עוֹלָמִים כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (זְבָחִים נד:) עַל פָּסוּק מְצָאנוּהָ בִּשְׂדֵה יָעַר.
— Therefore Benjamin is called ‘a ravening wolf,’ since the altar in the permanent Temple was built in his territory, as taught (Zevachim 54b) concerning ‘We found it in the field of the forest.’

וְעַל זֶה יֵשׁ לְרַמֵּז מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר וַיִּפּוֹל עַל צַוְּארֵי בִנְיָמִין אָחִיו וַיֵּבְךְּ וְגוֹמֵר וּפֵרֵשׁ רַבִּי שְׁלֹמֹה יִצְחָקִי (מִגְּמָרָא מְגִילָּה טז:) בָּכָה עַל שְׁנֵי מִקְדָּשִׁים שֶׁעֲתִידִין לִהְיוֹת בְּחֶלְקוֹ שֶׁל בִּנְיָמִין וּבִנְיָמִין בָּכָה עַל צַוָּארָיו עַל מִשְׁכַּן שִׁילֹה וְכוּלֵּי

— This may be alluded to in ‘He fell upon the neck of Benjamin his brother and wept,’ etc. Rashi explains, from Megillah 16b, that he wept over the two Temples destined to be in Benjamin's territory; ‘Benjamin wept upon his neck’ over the Tabernacle at Shiloh, etc.
כִּי עִיקַּר רֶמֶז הַצַּוָּאר הוּא עַל קְדוּשַּׁת הָאֲכִילָה וְהוּא עִנְיַן הַמִּקְדָּשׁ שֶׁהָיָה בּוֹ הַמִּזְבֵּחַ הַמְבָרֵר הָאֲכִילוֹת (וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנִּתְבָּאֵר מִקֵּץ מַאֲמָר ו)
— For the neck principally alludes to the holiness of eating. This is the meaning of the Temple, containing the altar that refines eating, as explained in Mikeitz, discourse 6.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Kedushat Shabbat 7:29: “A precious pearl hung from the neck of our father Abraham (Bava Batra 16b), for novel insights of Torah are called pearls… And this is spiritual eating, as it is said, ‘Come, eat of my bread.’ … This is why it says that the pearl hung from his neck, for there one hangs ornaments of precious stones and pearls, as it is written, ‘and chains for your throat.’ The throat is the place of swallowing, which is why a glutton is called by a name drawn from it (Ta'anit 24a), and that is the neck. Therefore they said (Megillah 16b) on the verse, ‘upon the neck of Benjamin his brother… and Benjamin wept upon his neck,’ that it alludes to the two Temples and the Tabernacle of Shiloh: for there was the altar that consumes all the offerings, which is why they said (Zevachim 53b) that it stood in the portion of the one who tears (‘Benjamin is a ravening wolf’). And this is the neck of holiness.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: Kedushat Shabbat gives the same chain: the neck is the place of swallowing, so the Temples on Benjamin's ‘neck’ are the altar that consumes the offerings in the portion of the ‘ravening wolf.’ It adds that the same neck held Abraham's pearl of Torah insight, so the holiness of eating at the altar is paired with the ‘spiritual eating’ of Torah.

p: וְהִנֵּה בְּפָרָשַׁת מִקֵּץ דִּכְתִיב וַיַּרְא יוֹסֵף אִתָּם אֶת בִּנְיָמִין וְגוֹמֵר כְּתִיב וַיְמַהֵר יוֹסֵף כִּי נִכְמְרוּ רַחֲמָיו אֶל אָחִיו וַיְבַקֵּשׁ לִבְכּוֹת וְגוֹמֵר
— In Parashat Mikeitz, where it says, ‘Joseph saw Benjamin with them,’ etc., it is written, ‘Joseph hurried, for his compassion toward his brother welled up, and he sought to weep,’ etc.
וְאָמַרְנוּ דְּהַיְינוּ מִפְּנֵי שֶׁרָאָה אֶת בִּנְיָמִין אִתָּם בִּבְחִינָתָם עַל עִנְיַן פִּלֶגֶשׁ בַּגִּבְעָה שֶׁחָלִילָה יִהְיֶה נֶחְסָר שִׁבְטוֹ עַל פְּגַם הַבְּרִית.
— We explained that he saw Benjamin with them in their spiritual state, concerning the episode of the concubine at Gibeah: his tribe might, Heaven forbid, be lost through a blemish of the covenant.
אָמְנָם לְאַחַר שֶׁנִּתְוַעֲדוּ הַשְּׁבָטִים בְּיַחַד וְנִתְגַּלּוּ זֶה לָזֶה קְדוּשַּׁת כָּל אֶחָד אָז נֶאֱמַר וַיִּפּוֹל עַל צַוְּארֵי בִנְיָמִין אָחִיו וַיֵּבְךְּ
— But after the tribes met together and each one's holiness was revealed to the others, it says, ‘He fell upon the neck of Benjamin his brother and wept.’
דְּיָדוּעַ שֶׁעִיקַּר פְּגַם הַבְּרִית נִמְשָׁךְ מִתַּאֲוַת אֲכִילָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁהָיָה רֵאשִׁית הַקִּלְקוּל בְּתַאֲוַת אֲכִילָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר וַתֵּרֶא הָאִשָּׁה כִּי טוֹב הָעֵץ לְמַאֲכָל

— For it is known that the blemish of the covenant stems primarily from the desire for food, just as the original corruption began through desire for food: ‘The woman saw that the tree was good for food.’
וּמִזֶּה נִמְשָׁךְ שֶׁבָּא נָחָשׁ עַל חַוָּה וְהֵטִיל בָּהּ זוּהֲמָא.
— From this followed the serpent's coming upon Eve and imparting defilement to her.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Et HaOchel §3: “Rectification of the desire for food comes first for a person, since it is somewhat easier for him; from it he proceeds to rectify the second desire [sexual desire]. Therefore the Sages placed tractate Nazir before tractate Sotah. In terms of perfection, however, perfection concerning the second desire is higher: since its punishment is greater, the greatness of its rectification is presumably also immense. For this reason the Torah places the passage of Sotah before that of Nazir, according to rank. The Sages reversed the order according to the human sequence of attaining that rank.”

h: Revealing the Shared Holiness of the Sanctuaries

p: אָמְנָם כְּשֶׁנִּתְוַדְּעוּ זֶה לָזֶה רָאָה יוֹסֵף בֶּאֱמֶת דְּבִנְיָמִין אָחִיו צַדִּיק לְתַתָּא (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב זֹהַר חֵלֶק א קנג ב) וּבֵית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ יִהְיֶה בָּנוּי בְּחֶלְקוֹ עִם הַמִּזְבֵּחַ

— Yet when they revealed themselves to one another, Joseph truly saw that his brother Benjamin was the lower righteous one (Zohar I, 153b), and that the Temple and its altar would be built in his territory.
וְזֶהוּ הַצַּוָּאר הָרוֹמֵז לִקְדוּשַּׁת הָאֲכִילָה אֲשֶׁר הוּא שַׁייָּכוּת לִקְדוּשַּׁת הַבְּרִית שֶׁלּוֹ הָרוֹמֵז עַל צַוַּאר מִשְׁכַּן שִׁילֹה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בְּחֶלְקוֹ
— This is the neck alluding to the holiness of eating, which is related to Joseph's holiness of the covenant, alluded to by the neck of the Tabernacle at Shiloh that would be in his territory.
וְאָז הִכִּירוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם אֶת בְּחִינָתָם שֶׁהוּא אֶחָד וְנִתְיַחֲדוּ. וּבָכוּ עַל שֶׁעֲתִידִין לֵיחָרֵב שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה גְמַר הַתִּיקּוּן עוֹד עַד עֵת בּוֹא קֵץ:

— Then both recognized that their spiritual aspects were one and became united. They wept because these sanctuaries were destined to be destroyed, and complete rectification would not come until the time of the end.

paragraphs.text: Zohar I, 153b: “Therefore Yosef and Binyamin are two righteous ones. Yosef merited to be the righteous one above because he guarded the sign of the covenant. Binyamin is the righteous one below, so that the Shemittah may be crowned between the two righteous ones, Yosef the righteous and Binyamin the righteous. Was Binyamin righteous? Yes, for all his days he never sinned against this sign of the covenant, although a trial like Yosef’s did not come his way. If so, why is he called righteous? Rather, throughout all the days that Yaakov mourned for Yosef, he did not engage in marital relations. If you say that when Yosef was taken from Yaakov, Binyamin was still a youth and unmarried, so how can you say that he refrained? Even after he subsequently married, he did not wish to engage in marital relations.”

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Maharal, Gur Aryeh, Bereishis 45:14: “‘Over two Temples,’ etc. As for why they wept now over the two Temples destined to be destroyed: in the Midrash, the weeping and the mutual recognition of the brothers was an allusion to Judah and Israel, that is, the Ten Tribes, whose head is Joseph, who will be made known to one another with weeping and supplication, as it is said, ‘With weeping they shall come, and with supplications I will lead them.’ This whole matter alludes to what is to come, for the fathers are always a sign for the children. Therefore it was alluded to now: when they make themselves known to one another, they weep over the troubles and destructions that came upon them, for Joseph one destruction, and for Benjamin two destructions.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: Maharal also ties the weeping to the moment the brothers made themselves known to one another, and reads it as a sign of a future reunion. Rav Tzadok names what that recognition showed, Benjamin's holiness of eating joined to Joseph's holiness of the covenant; Maharal reads the same moment as the future reunion of Judah with the Ten Tribes.
